Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Ghanaian rice quality has improved significantly – CSIR-CRI Chief Director Source : Albert Kuzor 17 November 2026 11:24am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Chief Research Scientist and Director at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research–Crops Research Institute (CSIR-CRI), Professor Maxwell Darko Asante, says the quality of locally produced rice has improved significantly, dismissing concerns that poor processing is responsible for its low patronage.
He said Ghana's rice industry has moved beyond the days when locally produced rice was commonly associated with stones and other impurities due to inadequate processing.
According to him, improvements in the country's rice production and processing systems have addressed some of the quality challenges that previously affected consumer confidence in local varieties.
"People talk about quality, but it is not true, we have gone past the quality issues long ago. Well, I should admit that a few times farmers don't treat the paddy well, and it doesn't mill well, but we have gone past the stage where there were stones in it," he said.
Prof. Asante said this on Joy FM's Super Morning Show , challenging the perception that Ghanaian rice is not selling because farmers and processors fail to sort their paddy or maintain acceptable quality standards properly.
He then attributed the low patronage of Ghanaian rice to the cheap importation of foreign rice, "the challenge we are facing is cheap import."
He maintained that the country's locally produced rice is now of good quality and should be able to compete with imported varieties on the market.
His comments come amid concerns about the growing dominance of imported rice and the difficulties local farmers face in selling their produce.
Prof. Asante has previously warned that the situation is discouraging farmers from continuing rice cultivation, with some reportedly abandoning the activity after struggling to sell their harvests.
He believes the challenges confronting local rice production require greater attention to market access and support for farmers to ensure that improvements in the quality of Ghanaian rice translate into increased patronage.
